words.def: Tending to talk a great deal.
words.simple: Talking a lot.
ex: After a glass of wine, the normally shy professor became quite [loquacious].
Our [loquacious] tour guide hardly paused for breath.
She was [loquacious] on every subject except her own past.
words.nuance: Loquacious is fairly neutral, even affectionate: someone who enjoys talking. Garrulous is more negative (talking too much about trivial things, often rambling); voluble means speaking fluently and at length, often with energy.
words.ety: Latin loquax 'talkative', from loqui 'to speak'.

prec.s: Usually quiet, the professor grew ___ after dinner, telling story after delightful story.
prec.why: Loquacious means talkative, neutral to positive — fitting 'delightful'. Garrulous implies tiresome rambling; verbose criticises using too many words; eloquent is about persuasive, beautiful expression, not quantity.

words.def: Fluent and persuasive in speaking or writing; clearly expressing a feeling.
words.simple: Speaking or writing in a clear and moving way.
ex: She made an [eloquent] plea for the refugees.
His silence was more [eloquent] than any words.
The poem speaks [eloquently] of loss.
words.nuance: Eloquent is about beautiful, moving expression. Articulate is about clarity — expressing ideas well. 'Eloquent testimony to' means 'clear evidence of'.
words.ety: Latin eloqui 'to speak out', from loqui 'to speak'.

prec.s: The empty classrooms were ___ testimony to the impact of the war on children.
prec.why: 'Eloquent testimony to' is a fixed phrase: powerfully expressive evidence. Articulate and fluent describe people speaking; verbal means expressed in words.

words.def: Using very few words.
words.simple: Using very few words.
ex: His [laconic] reply — 'No.' — ended the discussion.
The [laconic] cowboy is a classic figure of Western films.
She has a dry, [laconic] sense of humour.
words.nuance: Laconic often carries a sense of cool, dry wit. Terse can be rude or curt; succinct is praise for efficient expression; taciturn describes someone who rarely speaks at all.
words.ety: Greek Lakōnikos 'of Laconia' — the Spartans were famous for their brief speech.

prec.s: Asked how the expedition had gone, the explorer gave a ___ answer: 'Cold.'
prec.why: Laconic fits a dryly witty, extremely short reply. Succinct is praise for a clear summary; terse and curt suggest irritation or rudeness.

words.def: Using more words than are needed.
words.simple: Using more words than needed.
ex: The report is [verbose] and repetitive; cut it by half.
His [verbose] emails take ten minutes to read.
Legal documents are notorious for their [verbosity].
words.nuance: Verbose criticises writing or speech that uses too many words. Long-winded stresses boring length; prolix is a rare literary synonym.
words.ety: Latin verbosus, from verbum 'word'.

prec.s: The editor told him his essay was ___ and that every paragraph could lose a third of its words.
prec.why: Verbose describes text with too many words. Loquacious and garrulous describe talkative people, not texts; eloquent is praise.

words.def: Using many words to say something that could be said simply, especially to be vague or evasive.
words.simple: Using many words to avoid saying something simply.
words.easy: After a lot of [circumlocution], he finally said sorry.
ex: 'Negative patient outcome' is a hospital [circumlocution] for death.
After ten minutes of [circumlocution], he finally admitted he'd lost the money.
Politicians are masters of [circumlocution].
words.nuance: Circumlocution is talking around a subject. A euphemism is one mild word replacing a harsh one; circumlocution is a longer roundabout way of speaking.
words.ety: Latin circum 'around' + locutio 'speaking'.

prec.s: After a long ___ about 'restructuring' and 'optimising headcount', the manager admitted forty people would lose their jobs.
prec.why: Circumlocution means talking around the point to avoid saying it plainly. A digression or tangent wanders to a different topic; a diatribe is an angry attack.

words.def: (Of language) used in ordinary, informal conversation rather than formal speech or writing.
words.simple: Used in everyday talk, not in formal writing.
ex: 'Gonna' is [colloquial]; avoid it in your essay.
The novel is written in a lively, [colloquial] style.
The plant is known [colloquially] as 'mother-in-law's tongue'.
words.nuance: Colloquial is the neutral linguistic term for conversational language. Slang is more informal and often group-specific; vernacular means the everyday language of a region or group.
words.ety: Latin colloquium 'conversation', from loqui 'to speak'.

prec.s: The ant species is ___ known as the 'crazy ant' because of its erratic movement.
prec.why: 'Colloquially known as' is the standard phrase for a popular, everyday name. Vulgarly means coarsely (or, in old usage, 'commonly'); verbally means in spoken words; eloquently means expressively.

words.def: Deliberate exaggeration, not meant to be taken literally.
words.simple: Saying something is much bigger or worse than it is.
ex: Calling it 'the greatest film ever made' is pure [hyperbole].
Advertising is full of [hyperbole].
Without [hyperbole], this is the most important election in decades.
words.nuance: Hyperbole is exaggeration used deliberately for effect, a rhetorical device. Exaggeration is the general term; understatement is the opposite device.
words.ety: Greek huperbolē 'excess', from huper 'above' + ballein 'to throw'.

prec.s: 'I've told you a million times' is a classic example of ___.
prec.why: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect. A euphemism softens something unpleasant; irony says the opposite of what is meant; a metaphor describes one thing as another.

words.def: A mild or indirect word used instead of one that is harsh, blunt or embarrassing.
words.simple: A soft word used instead of an unpleasant one.
ex: 'Passed away' is a [euphemism] for 'died'.
'Collateral damage' is a chilling military [euphemism].
The company used the [euphemism] 'rightsizing' to describe mass layoffs.
words.nuance: A euphemism softens. A dysphemism does the opposite (a harsh term for something neutral). Circumlocution is a longer roundabout expression.
words.ety: Greek euphēmismos, from eu 'well' + phēmē 'speaking'.

prec.s: 'Between jobs' is a polite ___ for being unemployed.
prec.why: A euphemism replaces a blunt term with a gentle one. Hyperbole exaggerates; a cliché is an overused phrase; a metaphor is figurative comparison.

words.def: A remark that has been used too often to be interesting, especially one presented as wise.
words.simple: A boring thing people say too often.
ex: His speech was full of [platitudes] about 'working together'.
Grieving families don't need [platitudes]; they need answers.
'Everything happens for a reason' is a [platitude] I can't stand.
words.nuance: A platitude is a dull remark presented as if meaningful, often moral. A cliché is any overused phrase; a truism is a statement so obviously true it says nothing new.
words.ety: French plat 'flat', on the model of 'certitude'.

prec.s: Instead of concrete plans, the minister offered only empty ___ about 'building a brighter future'.
prec.why: 'Empty platitudes' is the classic phrase for hollow, moralising statements. Clichés are overused expressions in general; truisms are obviously true statements; slogans are short campaign phrases.

words.def: Expressing opinions or feelings loudly and forcefully.
words.simple: Loud and strong when giving your opinion.
words.easy: She's a [vociferous] critic of the plan.
ex: She was a [vociferous] critic of the war.
The plan met [vociferous] opposition from residents.
Fans protested [vociferously] against the ticket prices.
words.nuance: Vociferous stresses loudness and insistence in public opinion. Vocal is milder (expressing opinions openly); strident adds harshness and an unpleasant tone.
words.ety: Latin vociferari 'to shout', from vox 'voice' + ferre 'to carry'.

prec.s: The new airport faced ___ opposition, with thousands of residents protesting outside city hall.
prec.why: Vociferous opposition is loud and forceful. Eloquent is about fine expression; vigilant means watchful; verbose means wordy.

words.def: A forceful and bitter verbal attack against someone or something.
words.simple: A long, angry attack in words.
words.easy: He went on a [diatribe] about taxes.
ex: He launched into a long [diatribe] against modern art.
Her column was less a review than a [diatribe].
The speech became a [diatribe] against the media.
words.nuance: A diatribe is a bitter, sustained verbal or written attack. A tirade is a long angry speech, usually spoken; a rant is informal; invective is abusive language itself.
words.ety: Greek diatribē 'spending time, discourse'.

prec.s: Instead of reviewing the book, the critic wrote a 3,000-word ___ against the author's politics.
prec.why: A diatribe is a bitter, one-sided attack. A eulogy praises the dead; a critique is a balanced, reasoned assessment; satire mocks through humour.

words.def: An indirect remark that suggests something bad or sexual about someone.
words.simple: A hint that suggests something bad or sexual.
ex: The campaign relied on rumour and [innuendo] rather than facts.
The comedy is full of sexual [innuendo].
She was tired of the [innuendo] about how she got her job.
words.nuance: Innuendo is always suggestive and usually unpleasant — damaging hints or sexual double meanings. An allusion is a neutral indirect reference.
words.ety: Latin innuendo 'by nodding at', from innuere 'to nod towards'.

prec.s: The tabloids never accused her directly; they relied on rumour and ___.
prec.why: 'Rumour and innuendo' is a set pairing for damaging indirect suggestion. An allusion is a neutral indirect reference; an inference is a conclusion; an anecdote is a short story.

words.def: To suggest something unpleasant indirectly; to work oneself gradually into a position.
words.simple: To suggest something bad without saying it directly.
ex: Are you [insinuating] that I lied?
The article [insinuated] that the mayor had taken bribes.
He gradually [insinuated] himself into the family's affairs.
words.nuance: Insinuate implies a hidden, negative accusation. Imply is neutral; hint is light and can be positive.
words.ety: Latin insinuare 'to bring in by winding', from sinus 'curve'.

prec.s: 'Are you ___ that I stole the money?' she asked angrily.
prec.why: Insinuate is the natural verb for an indirect accusation, and 'Are you insinuating…?' is a typical angry response. Infer means conclude (the listener infers, not the speaker); allude needs 'to'; intimate is a formal neutral hint.

words.def: To mention something indirectly.
words.simple: To talk about something without naming it.
ex: She [alluded] to problems in her marriage but gave no details.
The title [alludes] to a poem by Yeats.
His speech was full of [allusions] to the Bible.
words.nuance: Allude means refer indirectly — the listener must catch the reference. Refer is direct. Don't confuse allusion with illusion (false perception) or elusion.
words.ety: Latin alludere 'to play with, refer to', from ludere 'to play'.

prec.s: The film's title ___ to a famous Shakespeare sonnet, though few viewers notice.
prec.why: Allude means refer indirectly, which is why 'few viewers notice'. Refers is direct; elicit means draw out a response; elude means escape.

words.def: To state or assert something firmly as a fact.
words.simple: To say firmly that something is true.
words.easy: The witness [averred] that she saw him.
ex: The witness [averred] that she had never seen the defendant before.
He [avers] that the documents are genuine.
Experts [aver] that the painting is a forgery.
words.nuance: Aver is formal or legal, with a sense of confident declaration of truth. Assert is the common equivalent; allege implies a claim without proof.
words.ety: Old French averer, from Latin verus 'true'.

prec.s: Under oath, the witness ___ that she had been at home all evening.
prec.why: Aver means declare firmly as true — suitable for sworn testimony. Allege is to accuse without proof; conjecture is to guess; imply is to suggest indirectly.

words.def: To admit that something is true, often reluctantly; to surrender or give up.
words.simple: To agree that something is true, even if you don't want to.
words.easy: He finally [conceded] that I was right.
ex: I [concede] that the plan has some weaknesses.
The candidate [conceded] defeat late on election night.
The team [conceded] two goals in the first ten minutes.
words.nuance: Concede implies reluctance — admitting something against your own interest or argument. Acknowledge is more neutral. In sport, you concede goals or points.
words.ety: Latin concedere 'to yield', from cedere 'to go'.

prec.s: With 90% of the votes counted, the senator finally ___ defeat.
prec.why: 'Concede defeat' is the fixed collocation in elections. Confess suggests guilt; surrender suggests war; relent means soften a harsh position and doesn't take an object.

words.def: To warn or reprimand someone firmly but mildly.
words.simple: To tell someone firmly that they did something wrong.
words.easy: The teacher [admonished] him for being late.
ex: The judge [admonished] the jury not to discuss the case.
She [admonished] her son for being rude to the waiter.
Despite repeated [admonitions], he kept arriving late.
words.nuance: Admonish is the gentlest of these: a serious warning or mild telling-off. Rebuke is sharper; castigate and lambaste are severe public criticism.
words.ety: Latin admonere 'to remind, warn'.

prec.s: The teacher gently ___ the boy for talking during the exam, then let him continue.
prec.why: Admonish fits a mild, firm warning — 'gently' signals it. Lambaste, castigate and berate all mean harsh, angry criticism.

words.def: To criticise or reprimand someone severely.
words.simple: To say very strongly that someone did wrong.
ex: The report [castigates] the government for its slow response.
She was [castigated] in the press for her comments.
Critics [castigated] the film as racist.
words.nuance: Castigate is formal, severe criticism, often in official reports or the press. Lambaste is more colourful; chastise can include physical punishment in older use.
words.ety: Latin castigare 'to correct, punish', from castus 'pure'.

prec.s: The official inquiry ___ the hospital management for ignoring repeated safety warnings.
prec.why: Castigate means severely criticise, fitting an official inquiry's damning verdict. Admonish is too mild; tease and nag are informal and personal.

words.def: To criticise someone or something very harshly.
words.simple: To attack someone with very harsh words in public.
ex: Critics [lambasted] the film as boring and overlong.
The coach [lambasted] his players after the defeat.
The minister was [lambasted] on social media.
words.nuance: Lambaste is vivid and common in journalism. Pan is used for reviews of films and shows; slam is headline-style informal.
words.ety: Probably from lam 'to beat' + baste 'to thrash'.

prec.s: After the 5–0 defeat, the furious manager ___ his players in front of the cameras.
prec.why: Lambaste means attack very harshly — suitable for a furious public outburst. Admonish and chide are mild; discourage means reduce someone's confidence or prevent.

words.def: To speak about someone or something as having little value or importance.
words.simple: To talk about someone as if they are not good or important.
ex: He never [disparaged] his rivals in public.
She made several [disparaging] remarks about her former employer.
Critics [disparaged] the novel as 'airport fiction'.
words.nuance: Disparage means to belittle — to make something seem unimportant or inferior. Denigrate is stronger, attacking reputation; belittle is the everyday word.
words.ety: Old French desparagier 'to marry someone of unequal rank'.

prec.s: His contract forbids him from making ___ remarks about the company for five years.
prec.why: 'Disparaging remarks' are belittling ones — a phrase common in legal agreements. Disparate means very different; desperate means hopeless; discerning means showing good judgement.

words.def: To praise someone or something enthusiastically.
words.simple: To praise something a lot.
ex: Doctors [extol] the virtues of regular exercise.
The article [extols] the city as a paradise for food lovers.
She was [extolled] as a hero after the rescue.
words.nuance: Extol is enthusiastic praise, often slightly overdone or promotional. 'Extol the virtues of' is a very common collocation, often ironic.
words.ety: Latin extollere 'to raise up'.

prec.s: Every wellness blogger seems to ___ the virtues of cold showers.
prec.why: 'Extol the virtues of' is the fixed collocation. Acclaim is used for works and achievements; applaud for actions; endorse means officially support.

words.def: To persuade someone to do something by flattery or gentle, persistent urging.
words.simple: To get someone to do something by being nice to them.
ex: She [cajoled] her brother into lending her his car.
The children [cajoled] their parents into buying a puppy.
Neither threats nor [cajolery] could change his mind.
words.nuance: Cajole uses flattery and persistence. Coax is gentle and patient (also with machines: coax an engine into life); wheedle is whiny and manipulative.
words.ety: French cajoler 'to chatter like a jay, flatter'.

prec.s: With compliments and promises, she ___ her reluctant boss into giving her Friday off.
prec.why: Cajole means persuade through flattery and charm. Coerce, compel and force all involve pressure or threats.

words.def: To make someone less angry or hostile, often by giving them something.
words.simple: To make someone less angry.
words.easy: He gave a refund to [placate] the customer.
ex: The airline offered free meals to [placate] angry passengers.
The concessions were designed to [placate] the unions.
Nothing could [placate] him once he'd lost his temper.
words.nuance: Placate means calming anger, often with a concession. Appease has a negative political sense (giving in to aggressors); mollify is softening anger, often with kind words.
words.ety: Latin placare 'to calm, appease'.

prec.s: To ___ furious customers, the airline offered everyone a free return flight.
prec.why: Placate means reduce someone's anger, often with a concession. Appease has a negative ring (giving in to unreasonable demands, especially in politics); pacify is often used for crying babies or violent regions; humour means go along with someone's wishes.

words.def: To calm someone's anger or anxiety; to soften.
words.simple: To calm someone who is angry or upset.
ex: Her apology did little to [mollify] the angry customer.
He seemed [mollified] by the promise of a refund.
The minister tried to [mollify] critics with a review of the policy.
words.nuance: Mollify is often used in the passive ('he was not mollified'), emphasising the softening of feelings. It is close to placate, but less about concessions.
words.ety: Latin mollificare, from mollis 'soft'.

prec.s: She apologised twice, but he did not seem ___ and kept glaring at her.
prec.why: Mollified (calmed, less angry) describes a person's feelings. Mitigated and alleviated apply to problems or pain, not people; subside is intransitive and describes things dying down.

words.def: To strongly encourage or urge someone to do something.
words.simple: To strongly tell people to do something.
words.easy: The coach [exhorted] the team to keep going.
ex: The coach [exhorted] his players to give everything in the second half.
The government [exhorted] citizens to save energy.
Despite constant [exhortations], few employees changed their habits.
words.nuance: Exhort suggests a passionate, public call to action, often from a leader. Implore is begging; urge is the everyday word.
words.ety: Latin exhortari, from hortari 'to encourage'.

prec.s: From the pulpit, the preacher ___ the congregation to give generously to the poor.
prec.why: Exhort is a leader's strong public encouragement. Implore and beseech mean begging desperately; extort means obtaining money by threats.

words.def: A person who takes part in a conversation or dialogue, especially an official one.
words.simple: The person you are talking with.
ex: She listens carefully to her [interlocutors] before replying.
Washington sees him as a reliable [interlocutor] with the regime.
In the dialogue, Socrates' [interlocutor] keeps changing his definition.
words.nuance: Interlocutor is formal; in diplomacy it means someone you can deal with on behalf of a group. In everyday speech, say 'the person you're talking to'.
words.ety: Latin interloqui 'to interrupt, speak between', from loqui 'to speak'.

prec.s: Western diplomats regard the deputy foreign minister as a credible ___ with the government.
prec.why: An interlocutor is a dialogue partner, especially in diplomacy. An interloper intrudes where not wanted; an intercessor pleads on someone's behalf; an interpreter translates.

words.def: To shock or excite someone into taking action.
words.simple: To shock or excite people so they act.
words.easy: The fire [galvanized] the town into action.
ex: The disaster [galvanized] the community into action.
Her speech [galvanized] young voters.
The goal [galvanized] the team, who scored twice more.
words.nuance: Galvanize suggests a sudden jolt of energy — like an electric shock. Mobilize is about organising people for action; spur is general encouragement.
words.ety: After Luigi Galvani, who made frogs' legs twitch with electricity.

prec.s: The shocking images of the oil spill ___ thousands of people into joining the protest.
prec.why: Galvanize into action describes a sudden surge of energy and motivation. Persuade is reasoned; induce is formal and neutral; provoke suggests anger or a reaction, often negative.

words.def: A political leader who gains support by exploiting people's emotions and prejudices rather than using reason.
words.simple: A leader who wins support with fear and anger, not facts.
ex: History is full of [demagogues] who blamed minorities for every problem.
Critics called the senator a dangerous [demagogue].
The campaign descended into [demagoguery].
words.nuance: A demagogue manipulates emotion and prejudice for power. A populist claims to represent ordinary people against elites (not always negative); a firebrand is a passionate agitator for a cause.
words.ety: Greek dēmagōgos 'leader of the people', from dēmos 'people' + agōgos 'leading'.

prec.s: The ___ won votes by blaming immigrants for every problem and promising easy solutions.
prec.why: A demagogue exploits prejudice and fear. A diplomat negotiates; a statesman is a respected, wise leader; a technocrat governs through technical expertise.

words.def: Strongly and often blindly supporting one party or cause; (n.) a committed supporter; a member of an armed resistance group.
words.simple: Strongly supporting one side or party.
ex: The debate has become bitterly [partisan].
The newspaper's coverage is openly [partisan].
The bill passed with [bipartisan] support.
words.nuance: Partisan is about loyalty to a party or side, especially in politics. Biased is more general unfairness; bipartisan means supported by both main parties.
words.ety: Italian partigiano, from parte 'part'.

prec.s: Healthcare reform has become so ___ that Democrats and Republicans can't agree on any detail.
prec.why: Partisan describes division along party lines. Prejudiced and discriminatory describe unfair attitudes to groups of people; subjective means based on personal feelings.

words.def: Leadership or dominance, especially by one state or social group over others.
words.simple: When one country or group has power over others.
words.easy: The empire kept its [hegemony] for years.
ex: The empire maintained its [hegemony] over the region for two centuries.
Some analysts predict the end of American [hegemony].
The tech giants' cultural [hegemony] worries regulators.
words.nuance: Hegemony is often used in political science for dominance that is partly accepted by the dominated (through culture and influence, not just force). Supremacy suggests being the highest; dominance is more general.
words.ety: Greek hēgemonia 'leadership', from hēgemōn 'leader'.

prec.s: Political scientists debate whether China will challenge the global ___ of the United States.
prec.why: Hegemony is dominance over others. Sovereignty is a state's authority over itself; jurisdiction is legal authority over an area; autonomy is self-government.

words.def: To deprive someone of the right to vote or of other rights; to make someone feel powerless.
words.simple: To take away someone's right to vote or to have a say.
words.easy: The new rule could [disenfranchise] poor voters.
ex: The new ID rules could [disenfranchise] thousands of elderly voters.
Many young people feel [disenfranchised] by mainstream politics.
The law effectively [disenfranchised] the country's poorest citizens.
words.nuance: Literally, disenfranchise means remove voting rights; figuratively it means make a group feel it has no voice. Marginalize means push to the edges of society.
words.ety: dis- + enfranchise, from Old French franc 'free'.

prec.s: Critics argue the new ID requirement will ___ poorer citizens who lack a passport or driving licence.
prec.why: Disenfranchise means take away voting rights — exactly what an ID requirement could do. Disinherit is about inheritance; dispossess is about property; displace is about forcing people from their homes.

words.def: Believing in or based on the principle that all people are equal and deserve equal rights.
words.simple: Believing that all people are equal.
words.easy: It's an [egalitarian] company with no private offices.
ex: Scandinavian countries are known for their [egalitarian] societies.
The company has an [egalitarian] culture with no private offices.
She is a committed [egalitarian].
words.nuance: Egalitarian is about equality of status and opportunity. Democratic is about government by the people; meritocratic is about rewarding ability.
words.ety: French égalitaire, from égal 'equal', from Latin aequalis.

prec.s: In their ___ office, the CEO sits at the same kind of desk as the newest intern.
prec.why: Egalitarian is about equal status for everyone. Meritocratic rewards ability; democratic is about voting and participation; uniform means all the same in form.

words.def: A system in which people are chosen and rewarded based on ability and achievement rather than wealth or class.
words.simple: A system where people move up because of skill, not money or family.
ex: The firm claims to be a [meritocracy], but most partners went to the same school.
Critics argue that [meritocracy] can justify inequality.
Entry to the civil service became more [meritocratic] in the 19th century.
words.nuance: Meritocracy is the ideal of rewarding talent and effort. Coined in 1958 as a satirical warning, it is now usually positive, though critics question whether it really exists.
words.ety: merit + -cracy (Greek kratos 'power').

prec.s: The startup prides itself on being a ___: anyone who delivers results gets promoted, regardless of degree.
prec.why: A meritocracy rewards ability. A bureaucracy runs on administrative rules; an aristocracy is rule by a hereditary elite; a plutocracy is rule by the rich.

words.def: The practice of people in power giving jobs or favours to relatives or friends.
words.simple: Giving jobs to your family members.
ex: Appointing his son as finance director was blatant [nepotism].
The film industry is often accused of [nepotism].
She got the job on merit, not through [nepotism].
words.nuance: Nepotism is favouritism toward family. Cronyism is favouritism toward friends and associates. In Hebrew, 'protektzia' covers both.
words.ety: Italian nepotismo, from nipote 'nephew' — popes gave posts to their 'nephews' (often their sons).

prec.s: When the president appointed his own daughter as ambassador, critics cried ___.
prec.why: Nepotism is specifically favouritism toward relatives. Cronyism is toward friends; bribery is paying for favours; patronage is the power to make appointments in general.

words.def: Kept secret or done secretly, especially because it is illegal or not approved.
words.simple: Secret, often because it is not allowed.
ex: They held [clandestine] meetings in a basement.
The agency ran a [clandestine] operation abroad.
Their [clandestine] affair lasted for years.
words.nuance: Clandestine describes organised secret activity, often illicit (meetings, operations, affairs). Surreptitious describes small secret actions done quietly to avoid notice (a surreptitious glance).
words.ety: Latin clandestinus, from clam 'secretly'.

prec.s: Resistance members held ___ meetings in a church cellar to plan their operations.
prec.why: Clandestine fits organised secret activity like meetings and networks. Surreptitious and furtive describe small, quick actions (a glance, a sip); stealthy describes quiet movement.

words.def: Done secretly or quietly so that others won't notice.
words.simple: Done quietly so no one sees.
words.easy: She took a [surreptitious] look at her phone.
ex: She took a [surreptitious] look at her phone during the meeting.
He [surreptitiously] slipped the note into her bag.
The [surreptitious] recording was later used in court.
words.nuance: Surreptitious is about small sneaky actions. Furtive adds guilt or nervousness; covert is used for official secret operations.
words.ety: Latin surrepticius 'obtained secretly', from surripere 'to snatch secretly'.

prec.s: During the long speech, he took a ___ glance at the football score on his phone.
prec.why: Surreptitious suits small, quick secret actions like a glance. Clandestine and covert suit organised operations; conspicuous means easily noticed — the opposite.

words.def: Trying to undermine an established system or authority.
words.simple: Trying to weaken the people in power.
ex: The regime banned books it considered [subversive].
Her comedy has a quietly [subversive] edge.
The film [subverts] the usual romantic clichés.
words.nuance: Subversive can be political (dangerous to the state) or artistic (cleverly undermining conventions, often praise). Seditious is the legal term for inciting rebellion against the state.
words.ety: Latin subvertere 'to overturn', from vertere 'to turn'.

prec.s: Behind its cheerful songs, the musical has a quietly ___ message about class and power.
prec.why: Subversive suits art that cleverly undermines conventions. Seditious and treasonous are legal or political crimes against the state; mutinous describes soldiers or crews rebelling.

words.def: Proceeding gradually and subtly, but with harmful effects.
words.simple: Harmful and growing slowly without people noticing.
ex: High blood pressure is an [insidious] disease with few early symptoms.
Prejudice can be [insidious], shaping decisions without our awareness.
The [insidious] spread of misinformation online worries researchers.
words.nuance: Insidious stresses the hidden, gradual nature of harm. Pernicious stresses the severity of the harm — often also gradual.
words.ety: Latin insidiosus 'cunning', from insidiae 'ambush'.

prec.s: Glaucoma is ___: it slowly damages your sight for years before you notice anything.
prec.why: Insidious means harmful while progressing unnoticed. Virulent means highly infectious or hostile; acute means sudden and severe; malignant means cancerous or evil.

words.def: Having a harmful effect, especially gradually or in a way that is not obvious.
words.simple: Very harmful, often in a hidden way.
ex: The [pernicious] influence of corruption spread through every ministry.
Debt can have a [pernicious] effect on mental health.
This is a [pernicious] myth that deserves to die.
words.nuance: Pernicious emphasises deep, destructive harm, especially to morals or society. Insidious emphasises stealth.
words.ety: Latin perniciosus 'destructive', from pernicies 'ruin', from nex 'death'.

prec.s: The idea that poor people deserve their poverty is a ___ myth that shapes cruel policies.
prec.why: 'Pernicious myth/influence' are strong collocations for ideas that do deep harm. Noxious is used for gases and fumes; toxic for poisons (and informally for relationships); deleterious is technical (deleterious effects on health).

words.def: To exclude someone from a group or society.
words.simple: To push someone out of a group.
words.easy: She was [ostracized] for telling the truth.
ex: She was [ostracized] by her colleagues after reporting the fraud.
Children who are different are often [ostracized] at school.
He feared social [ostracism] if he came out.
words.nuance: Ostracize means exclusion by a group. Shun is avoiding someone; marginalize is pushing to the edges of power or importance, not necessarily social rejection.
words.ety: Greek ostrakizein — Athenians voted to banish citizens by writing names on pottery shards (ostraka).

prec.s: After he broke the strike, his neighbours ___ him: nobody spoke to him for years.
prec.why: Ostracize means social exclusion by a group. Marginalize means reduce someone's importance or influence; persecute means harass or punish; banish means send away officially.

words.def: To treat a person, group or idea as unimportant or push them to the edge of society.
words.simple: To treat a person or group as not important.
ex: The reform aims to help [marginalized] communities.
Women's contributions to science were long [marginalized].
The party has been [marginalized] since the election.
words.nuance: Marginalize is about reducing power or importance. Sideline is more informal, especially at work; ostracize is social rejection.
words.ety: From margin, Latin margo 'edge'.

prec.s: For decades, history textbooks ___ the role of women in the scientific revolution.
prec.why: Marginalize means treat as unimportant — fitting for contributions or roles. Ostracize is social exclusion of people; excommunicate is expulsion from a church; evict is removal from a home.

words.def: A person or group blamed for the faults or failures of others.
words.simple: Someone blamed for what others did.
words.easy: They made him the [scapegoat] for the failure.
ex: The junior manager was made a [scapegoat] for the company's failure.
Immigrants are often [scapegoated] in times of economic crisis.
The coach became the [scapegoat] for the team's poor season.
words.nuance: A scapegoat takes the blame for others. Fall guy and patsy (informal) suggest someone set up or tricked into taking the blame.
words.ety: From the Hebrew Bible (Leviticus 16): the goat sent into the wilderness carrying the people's sins — 'Azazel'.

prec.s: When the project failed, management made the newest employee the ___ to protect themselves.
prec.why: A scapegoat is blamed unfairly for others' failures. A martyr suffers for a cause; a culprit is actually guilty; an underdog is expected to lose.

words.def: Excessive pride or self-confidence, often leading to downfall.
words.simple: Too much pride that leads to failure.
ex: The CEO's [hubris] led him to ignore every warning.
Building the 'unsinkable' Titanic was an act of [hubris].
It would be [hubristic] to declare victory so early.
words.nuance: Hubris is pride that tempts fate and brings punishment — from Greek tragedy. Arrogance is the everyday term without the sense of downfall. Nemesis is the punishment that follows.
words.ety: Greek hubris 'insolence, outrage'.

prec.s: Calling the ship 'unsinkable' was an act of ___ that history would punish.
prec.why: Hubris is overconfidence that invites disaster — the tragic dimension the sentence describes. Vanity is pride in appearance; arrogance and conceit lack the sense of punishment by fate.

words.def: The general mood, ideas and beliefs typical of a particular period of history.
words.simple: The mood and ideas of a time.
words.easy: The song caught the [zeitgeist] of its time.
ex: The novel captured the [zeitgeist] of the 1920s.
Her songs seem to tap into the [zeitgeist].
Anxiety about technology is part of today's [zeitgeist].
words.nuance: Zeitgeist is the spirit of a particular time. Ethos is the characteristic spirit of a group or institution; climate is the current state of opinion.
words.ety: German Zeit 'time' + Geist 'spirit'.

prec.s: Few films capture the ___ as well as this one, which perfectly reflects the anxieties of its decade.
prec.why: The zeitgeist is the spirit of a particular time — 'capture the zeitgeist' is the set phrase. Ethos is a group's character; milieu is a social environment; vogue is a passing fashion.

words.def: Not securely held or in position; dangerously uncertain.
words.simple: Not safe or stable; it could fall or fail.
ex: Many freelancers live a [precarious] existence.
The vase was balanced [precariously] on the edge of the shelf.
The country's economy is in a [precarious] state.
words.nuance: Precarious means in danger of falling or failing at any moment. Perilous means full of danger; tenuous is about weak connections, not instability.
words.ety: Latin precarius 'obtained by asking, uncertain', from prex 'prayer'.

prec.s: Without a contract or savings, gig workers lead a ___ existence from month to month.
prec.why: 'A precarious existence' is the classic phrase for insecure living. Tenuous is used for links and grips; perilous for dangerous journeys or situations; volatile for prices and tempers.

words.def: Regularly found in a particular place, group or situation; (of plants and animals) native to one area.
words.simple: Always found in a place or group.
ex: Malaria is [endemic] in parts of Africa.
Corruption was [endemic] in the old regime.
The island has dozens of [endemic] bird species.
words.nuance: Endemic means always present in a place or group. An epidemic is a sudden outbreak; pandemic is worldwide. Systemic means built into the whole system.
words.ety: Greek endēmos 'native', from en 'in' + dēmos 'people'.

prec.s: Bribery was so ___ in the old customs service that nothing moved without a payment.
prec.why: Endemic means permanently present in a place or group. Epidemic and pandemic describe sudden widespread outbreaks; sporadic means occasional.

words.def: Relating to or affecting an entire system rather than just individual parts.
words.simple: Affecting the whole organization, not just one part.
words.easy: The problem is [systemic], not one bad person.
ex: The report found [systemic] failures in the child-protection service.
The crisis exposed [systemic] risk in the banking sector.
This isn't one bad officer; the problem is [systemic].
words.nuance: Systemic means built into a whole system. Systematic means methodical, done according to a plan — a common confusion.
words.ety: From system, Greek sustēma 'organised whole'.

prec.s: The inquiry found that the failures weren't one person's fault but ___, built into how the hospital was run.
prec.why: Systemic means affecting the whole system. Systematic and methodical mean done according to a careful method; chronic means long-lasting.

words.def: (Of laws or measures) excessively harsh and severe.
words.simple: Much too harsh.
ex: The government introduced [draconian] laws against protest.
Critics called the spending cuts [draconian].
The school's [draconian] dress code banned coloured socks.
words.nuance: Draconian criticises rules or punishments as far too harsh. Strict can be neutral or positive; punitive means intended as punishment.
words.ety: From Draco, a 7th-century BC Athenian lawgiver whose code punished even small crimes with death.

prec.s: Under the new ___ laws, even minor protest could lead to five years in prison.
prec.why: Draconian criticises laws as excessively harsh, out of proportion. Stringent and rigorous mean strict and thorough, often approvingly; austere means plain and severe in style.

words.def: Freedom from punishment or harmful consequences.
words.simple: Without being punished.
ex: Gangs operated with [impunity] in the city's poorer districts.
You can't break the rules with [impunity] forever.
The report condemned the culture of [impunity] in the police force.
words.nuance: Impunity is almost always used in 'with impunity' and implies injustice. Immunity is an official, often legal, protection (diplomatic immunity).
words.ety: Latin impunitas, from in- 'not' + poena 'penalty'.

prec.s: For years, the warlords committed crimes with ___, knowing no court would touch them.
prec.why: 'With impunity' means without being punished, implying injustice. Immunity is formal legal protection; indemnity is insurance-style compensation; amnesty is an official pardon.

words.def: Involved with others in wrongdoing, actively or by silence.
words.simple: Helping something bad happen, even by staying quiet.
ex: By staying silent, the board was [complicit] in the fraud.
Several officials were [complicit] in the cover-up.
She denied any [complicity] in the scheme.
words.nuance: Complicit means sharing moral responsibility — including by doing nothing. Implicated means shown to be involved, especially by evidence; an accomplice actively helps commit a crime.
words.ety: From complicity, French complicité, from Latin complicare 'to fold together'.

prec.s: Those who knew about the abuse and said nothing were, in a sense, ___ in it.
prec.why: 'Complicit in' captures moral participation, even through silence. Implicated means shown by evidence to be involved; accomplice is a noun; culpable means deserving blame and takes 'for', not 'in'.

words.def: To accept something reluctantly but without protest.
words.simple: To agree quietly, even if you don't want to.
ex: The board reluctantly [acquiesced] to the shareholders' demands.
She [acquiesced] in the decision, though she thought it was wrong.
His [acquiescence] was taken as approval.
words.nuance: Acquiesce stresses passive acceptance without enthusiasm. Accede is formal agreement to a request; comply is following rules or orders.
words.ety: Latin acquiescere 'to rest, be at peace', from quies 'quiet'.

prec.s: Too tired to argue any longer, he finally ___ to his children's demands for a puppy.
prec.why: Acquiesce means give in quietly and reluctantly, and takes 'to/in'. Accord means give or agree; concede usually takes an object (concede defeat); concur means agree in opinion.
